questions.stem: Tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean are named by:

options.option_text: The NOAA (USA)
A rotational list maintained by 13 member countries
Random auto-naming by AI
The country where cyclone first makes landfall

questions.explanation: RSMC New Delhi (IMD) is the regional specialised meteorological centre for the N. Indian Ocean. 13 member countries contribute names — current list released 2020, 169 names. Arrival order: Amphan, Nisarga, Gati, Nivar, Tauktae, Yaas, Biparjoy etc. RSMC New Delhi — IMD.

questions.explanation: Tropical-cyclone names by region: Hurricane (Atlantic, NE Pacific — USA, Caribbean, Mexico). Typhoon (NW Pacific — Japan, Philippines). Cyclone (N. Indian Ocean — Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea; S. Pacific — Australia). Willy-willy (local term in Australia, less official).

options.option_text: Flows of magma underground
Fast, narrow air currents in the upper troposphere / lower stratosphere
Tropical ocean currents
Air bubbles in boiling water

questions.explanation: Jet streams — ~9-16 km altitude — narrow bands of very fast west-to-east winds (often > 200 km/h). Key types: Subtropical, Polar front jets. Westerly jet in summer also Tropical Easterly Jet. Affect monsoon, cyclones, aviation.

questions.stem: Match the LOCAL WIND with its location. A. Sirocco.  B. Mistral.  C. Chinook.  D. Loo. List-II: 1. Sahara/Mediterranean (hot, dusty).  2. France/Mediterranean (cold N-W).  3. Rocky Mountains, USA (warm, dry).  4. Northern India (hot summer).
questions.explanation: Sirocco — hot, dusty wind from Sahara blowing across Mediterranean. Mistral — cold, north-westerly wind in Rhone valley, France. Chinook — 'snow eater' wind descending leeward side of Rockies — warm & dry. Loo — hot summer wind in northern India.
questions.subject: Geography

options.option_text: Winter, in Punjab
Pre-monsoon (Apr-May) in West Bengal, Odisha, Bangladesh
Monsoon season in Kerala
Autumn in Kashmir

questions.explanation: Norwesters / Kalbaishakhi ('Baisakh-month storm') — pre-monsoon convective thunderstorms over eastern India (WB, Jharkhand, Odisha) and Bangladesh. Bring hailstorms but also brief rainfall that helps jute, rice, mangoes ('mango showers' in Kerala/Karnataka are similar pre-monsoon phenomena).

questions.stem: The eye of a tropical cyclone is characterised by:

options.option_text: Strongest winds and heaviest rain
Calm weather with little wind and often clear sky
Snow and freezing temperatures
Thunderstorms and lightning

questions.explanation: Eye = calm, low-pressure centre of a tropical cyclone (~30-65 km across). Clear or partly clear. Surrounded by the eyewall — the most violent region (strongest winds, heaviest rain). Under the eye, there is a brief calm before the winds return from the opposite direction as the other eyewall passes overhead.

questions.stem: The Beaufort Wind Scale, still referenced in marine weather bulletins worldwide, was originally devised to estimate wind speed by observing?

options.option_text: Barometric pressure readings taken at coastal weather stations
Observable sea-state and wave behaviour as reported by sailors
Anemometer recordings at standardised meteorological observatories
Radiosonde balloon measurements collected at the 850 hPa pressure level

questions.explanation: Rear Admiral Francis Beaufort devised the scale in 1805 so ship officers could estimate wind speed from sea-state and wave observations without instruments, assigning numbers 0–12 to visible conditions. Barometric pressure (A) and anemometers (C) measure wind but were not the original basis of the scale; radiosondes (D) were not invented until 1930.

questions.stem: The 'Doldrums', notorious among early seafarers for becalming sailing ships for days or weeks at a stretch, correspond to which atmospheric feature?

options.option_text: Sub-tropical high-pressure belt situated around 30° north and south
Polar front low-pressure zone found at approximately 60°N and 60°S
Equatorial low-pressure belt where northeast and southeast trade winds converge
Temperate westerlies zone lying between latitudes 40°S and 60°S

questions.explanation: The Doldrums coincide with the ITCZ near the equator, where converging trade winds produce calm air and weak variable breezes that left sailing ships stranded. Option A describes the 'Horse Latitudes' — another calm belt at ~30° caused by descending air in the Hadley Cell, which is frequently confused with the Doldrums in exams.

questions.stem: The 'Föhn' effect produces a warm, dry wind on the leeward side of a mountain range primarily because?

options.option_text: Latent heat released during condensation is retained as air descends the leeward slope
Intense solar radiation at high altitude heats the air before its descent begins
Coriolis deflection accelerates airflow and raises air temperature near the surface
Orographic cooling on the windward side draws stored thermal energy from ocean moisture

questions.explanation: On the windward slope, rising air cools at the saturated adiabatic lapse rate (~6°C/km) once condensation begins, losing moisture as precipitation. On the leeward side the now-drier air descends and warms at the faster dry adiabatic rate (~10°C/km), arriving warmer and drier than the original air at the same altitude. Solar radiation (B) and Coriolis (C) play no role in this thermodynamic mechanism.

questions.stem: The Walker Circulation in the equatorial Pacific weakens or reverses during El Niño events primarily because?

options.option_text: Eastern Pacific warming flattens the pressure gradient that normally drives trade winds
Polar jet streams shift equatorward and disrupt the trade wind circulation system
The ITCZ migrates permanently southward across the equator, blocking trade wind flow
Higher solar output during El Niño years directly warms the eastern Pacific Ocean

questions.explanation: Normally the western Pacific is warmer (low pressure) and the eastern Pacific (Peru coast) is cooler (high pressure); this east-west gradient drives easterly trade winds and sustains the Walker Cell. El Niño's anomalous eastern Pacific warming reduces this gradient, weakening or reversing the circulation. Polar jets (B) operate at much higher latitudes and are not the primary mechanism; El Niño has no proven solar-output link (D).

questions.stem: The intense thermal low that develops over the Thar Desert during May–June contributes to the onset of the Indian Summer Monsoon mainly by?

options.option_text: Cooling the upper troposphere to initiate deep convection over the Bay of Bengal
Shifting the subtropical westerly jet stream northward across the Tibetan Plateau
Generating dust-loaded convective clouds that seed rainfall across northwest India
Creating a steep land-to-sea pressure gradient that draws moisture-laden winds inland

questions.explanation: The Thar heat low (surface pressure ~994 hPa) versus relatively higher oceanic pressure over the Arabian Sea sets up a strong land-to-sea pressure gradient that 'pulls' moisture-laden southwest winds deep into the subcontinent — the classic thermal-low suction mechanism. The jet stream shift (B) is a separate upper-level trigger; it is the Tibetan heating, not the Thar low, that forces the jet northward.

questions.stem: The abrupt northward withdrawal of the subtropical westerly jet stream from over the Indian subcontinent in late May is regarded as a key upper-level precondition for which event?

options.option_text: Onset of the southwest monsoon over the Kerala coast in early June
Retreat of the northeast monsoon from the Tamil Nadu coast in late December
Formation of pre-monsoon tropical cyclones in the northern Bay of Bengal
Development of western disturbances over the northwest Himalayan foothills

questions.explanation: During winter and spring, the southern branch of the subtropical westerly jet (~200 hPa) lies over peninsular India (~25°N), acting as an upper-level barrier that suppresses northward moisture advance. As the Tibetan Plateau heats intensely in late May, this jet shifts beyond 35°N, removing the barrier and permitting the southwest monsoon to burst over Kerala. Western disturbances (D) are in fact steered by this same jet in its winter position — the confusion between its active and withdrawn phases is the most tempting distractor.

questions.stem: In the life cycle of a mid-latitude extratropical cyclone, the stage called 'occlusion' refers to the process where?

options.option_text: The cyclone fully dissipates as its low-pressure core fills with descending cold air
Upper-level wind shear splits the system into two separate rotating vortices
The faster-moving cold front overtakes the warm front, lifting warm sector air aloft
Two cyclones merge along a stationary front, amplifying the central pressure drop

questions.explanation: As the cyclone matures, the cold front (which travels faster) catches up with the warm front, squeezing the warm sector air upward off the surface to form an occluded front. The system typically weakens after this point, but option A describes the subsequent filling stage — not occlusion itself. The Bergen School cyclone model (Bjerknes, 1919) explicitly identifies occlusion as stage three in the cyclone life cycle, making A the most plausible wrong choice in an exam setting.
